scoring.rule: An answer passes when every key point in `required` is present and, if `any_of` is not empty, at least one of those too. Any `fail_if` match fails the answer whatever else it says. A `recitation_flags` phrase used without the mechanism behind it triggers one follow-up instead of a pass.

pairs.question: A classmate's spec opens with: "Working professionals waste a lot of time on reports, and AI can help." Compare it with: "Every Friday Aarav opens Jira, reads the week's tickets, writes a status report and posts it on Slack. It takes him about 90 minutes." Which one is an observation, and what does the first one leave you unable to do?

key_points.text: The second is the observation: a specific, real person's struggle that was actually seen, with what they do and how long it takes.
The first is an assumption about a crowd. With no real person or task in it, you cannot do the job by hand, write a golden pair or check whether the output helped anyone.
A good observation also shows the struggle has no working solution yet, so it is worth building for.

fail_if: Picks the first statement as the observation
Says both are equally good observations

pairs.source: Concept summary; Lecture 4 notes (Aarav's Friday report)

pairs.question: Your team writes the hypothesis: "Our app will help early-career people get better at AI." A mentor says you can never be proven wrong with that sentence. Why not, and rewrite it so a test with real users could fail it.

key_points.text: There is no number or outcome to check, so any result can be read as success.
A testable hypothesis names an assumed cause and a measurable result with a number, such as: given a workflow diagnosis, 6 of 10 early-career people map one repeated workflow and build an app.
The hypothesis also decides what is worth storing and measuring, because you only store what tests the bet.

fail_if: Rewrite still has no number or observable outcome

pairs.source: Concept summary; Lecture 8 notes (the 6 of 10 bet)

pairs.question: The diagnose app returned a plan full of Python code. It ran without errors. If your spec said the user was "working professionals", would you know this plan was wrong? What changes when the spec says the user is Aarav, a 26-year-old business analyst in Pune?

key_points.text: With a vague crowd as the user there is nothing to judge the output against, so a plan full of code can look fine.
Aarav is a business analyst who cannot read Python yet, so a code-heavy plan is useless to him. A named user makes that failure visible.
It leads to a concrete prompt change: no jargon, one step at a time, the minimum action needed now.

fail_if: Says the plan is fine because the code runs

pairs.question: Aarav says writing client emails is slow. Gmail already drafts emails for him, and he uses it happily. Is "Aarav writes emails slowly" a good observation to build on? What would you need to see before it is?

key_points.text: No. A good observation is a struggle with no working solution, and Gmail already solves this one for him.
You would need to see where the existing solution fails him in practice, for example a step Gmail cannot do, before it is worth building.

fail_if: Says yes, build it, without addressing the existing solution

pairs.question: Your teammate tests the diagnose app by reading each output and saying "looks good". What should they compare the output against instead, and where does that come from?

key_points.text: Golden pairs: an ideal input and the ideal output for it.
They are written by doing the job by hand after talking to real users, before you see what the model produces.
"Looks good" changes with mood and with who is reading. A golden pair is the same check every time.

fail_if: Suggests asking the model whether its output is good

pairs.question: A team's verifier reads: "The plan is good if Aarav likes it." Why is that weak? Write a better one that uses a threshold and a baseline.

key_points.text: A verifier is a written condition you can check. "Aarav likes it" is a feeling, can change run to run, and cannot be applied without him.
A better one sets a threshold, for example 8 of 10 golden pairs meet the written condition.
It compares against a baseline, such as the raw model with no prompt or the previous prompt, so you know the change helped.

fail_if: New verifier is still a feeling or opinion with no number

pairs.question: Bhavani's code was the only one in class that ran, and it returned a plan. It still failed. If "the code runs" is not the verifier, what is, and what did checking against it change?

key_points.text: Working is not the same as useful. The verifier checks whether the output helps the user, not whether the code runs.
The plan was full of code that Aarav cannot read, so it failed for him.
The check forced a prompt change: no jargon, one step at a time, the minimum action needed now.

fail_if: Says it passed because it ran

pairs.question: You are about to write diagnose(workflow). Your friend opens Cursor and starts prompting for code. What should you write first, and why in plain English rather than code?

key_points.text: First write the input, the expected output and the process in English, including the test the output has to pass.
You cannot write the process for a problem you have not done by hand, and an English test can be checked before any code exists.
The code is then done when it meets that test. You can even mock the model and build the deterministic path from the golden pair first.

fail_if: Says to write code first and test later

pairs.source: Concept summary; Lecture 5 notes, section 01; Lecture 7 notes, section 10

pairs.question: In your Concept Check app, after the follow-up you ask the model: "Does the learner understand now?" It says yes for 9 out of 10 learners. Why can't you trust that number, and what should decide instead?

key_points.text: A model asked that question tends to say yes, kindly, to almost everyone. It is a soft judge.
A new case with an answer written before the session should decide. Code compares the learner's answer to that answer key.

fail_if: Suggests a better prompt for the same yes/no question as the fix

pairs.question: Pick search, form or chat for each, and say why: (a) Aarav wants to find a past diagnosis that mentioned Jira. (b) A user submits a refund request with an order ID and a reason. (c) Aarav describes a messy workflow he can't quite explain and needs help pinning down.

key_points.text: (a) Search: the thing already exists and he is finding it.
(b) Form: the inputs are known and fixed, so fields capture them exactly.
(c) Chat: the input is open-ended and needs back-and-forth to pin down.

fail_if: Picks chat for all three

pairs.question: Gradio gives you a working chat UI in about four lines of Python. What is it hiding from you, and describe a moment when not knowing that would hurt.

key_points.text: Gradio is a cushion over HTML, CSS and JavaScript: a text area, a button, an output box and a request to the backend.
When something breaks or lands on the wrong machine, such as a key ending up in the browser, you need to know what is underneath to fix it.

fail_if: Says Gradio is the backend or calls the model by itself

pairs.question: Your Gradio chat for Aarav runs and replies with exactly what he typed. The UI works. What is missing, and why can't you just ask an AI to fill it in yet?

key_points.text: Input and output exist but there is no process: the step that turns his workflow into a plan he can use.
You cannot write the process for a problem you have not done by hand. Run the loop manually first to learn what a good output is.

fail_if: Says nothing is missing because it runs

pairs.question: Before writing any code, you offer Aarav this: he sends his workflow on WhatsApp and you send a diagnosis back by hand within an hour. Your friend calls it a waste of time. What do you get from doing it by hand that code can't give you yet?

key_points.text: It proves the input, process and output loop is useful to a real person before you build anything.
Each round gives you a real golden pair and shows you the process, which becomes your prompt.
It is cheap to change. Fixing a manual process costs a message, not a rebuild.

fail_if: Agrees it is a waste of time

pairs.question: Aarav's UI sends a request to https://diagnosis.aarav.dev/aarav/diagnosis (singular). The real door is /aarav/diagnoses. The method, key and body are all correct. What comes back? Is the problem in the part that names the machine or the part that names the door?

key_points.text: 404 Not Found.
The domain is right, so the machine was reached. The path names a door that doesn't exist.
Fixing the method, key or body won't help, because only the address is wrong.

fail_if: Says 401, 400 or a 5xx
Says the server is down

pairs.question: Aarav's /aarav/diagnoses door accepts only CREATE and READ. His UI sends a DELETE there, with the right key. What comes back, and why is the address not the problem?

key_points.text: 405 Method Not Allowed.
The door exists. The server just doesn't allow that action at it.
The method tells the server what to do with the thing at the address, so one URL can behave differently for different methods.

fail_if: Says 404 or wrong URL

pairs.question: A teammate puts the Groq key in the React code so the browser calls Groq directly and skips the backend. It works on their laptop. What can any visitor to the site now do, and why doesn't Groq notice it isn't you?

key_points.text: Anything the page sends, a visitor can read in DevTools or the Network tab, so the key is public.
"Bearer" means whoever holds the key gets in. Groq checks the key, not the person.
Others spend your limit (30 a minute, 1,000 a day) and your bill. The fix is to keep the key in a backend environment variable.

fail_if: Suggests hiding or minifying the key in frontend code, or a frontend .env, as the fix

pairs.question: Aarav's service expects {"workflow": "..."}. Your UI sends the body as a plain sentence: "I open Jira, read the week's tickets..." What comes back, and why can't the server just read the sentence?

key_points.text: 400 Bad Request.
The server doesn't guess the format. Both sides must agree on it: JSON with the named field.
The Content-Type: application/json header tells the server the body is JSON.

pairs.question: Aarav wants his app to email him each new plan using Resend, a service you have never used. Before you read a line of its code, what four things do you need to find out? Give your best guess for each.

key_points.text: Address: the endpoint, for example POST https://api.resend.com/emails.
Action: POST, because sending an email creates something new.
Key: an API key from Resend, sent in the Authorization header from the backend.
Package: a JSON body with from, to, subject and the message.

fail_if: Says the key goes in the frontend

pairs.source: Lecture 5 notes, section 15; Lecture 6 notes, section 01

pairs.question: A Google search puts your question in the address bar and uses GET. Asking a model on Groq uses POST, with your prompt in the body. A friend says the model call should be a GET, since you're "just getting an answer". What's wrong with that?

key_points.text: GET reads what already exists. Google's results already sit in its index, and nothing new is stored.
The model creates a reply that didn't exist before (ask twice and you get two different replies), so it's a Create, which is POST.
The prompt can be long and private, so it goes in the body, not the address.

recitation_flags: POST is for sending data, GET is for retrieving
fail_if: Agrees it should be a GET

pairs.question: Workflow 7 has three fields: title, frequency "weekly" and steps. Aarav sends {"frequency": "every Friday"} twice: once as PATCH /workflows/7, once as PUT /workflows/7. What does workflow 7 look like after each request?

key_points.text: After PATCH, only frequency changes. Title and steps stay.
After PUT, the whole workflow is replaced, so title and steps are lost, because the body only had frequency.
Both are Update. PUT needs the full object.

fail_if: Says both give the same result

pairs.question: A teammate builds the Remove button as a link to GET /deleteWorkflow?id=7. It works. Why is DELETE /workflows/7 the better request, and what could go wrong with the GET version?

key_points.text: GET is meant to read what exists and change nothing. Using it to delete breaks that promise.
Anything that follows links or preloads pages, such as a browser, a link preview or a crawler, could send that GET and delete data by accident.
The address should name the thing (/workflows/7) and the method should name the action (DELETE).

fail_if: Says both are equally fine because it works

pairs.source: Lecture 4 notes (CRUD rule; REST gave nouns and CRUD)

pairs.question: You paste https://api.groq.com/openai/v1/chat/completions into your browser's address bar and press Enter. It fails. The address is correct. Why can't the address bar make this call, and what do you use instead?

key_points.text: The address bar only sends GET.
This endpoint needs a POST with a JSON body and an Authorization header, and the address bar can't add either.
Use a tool that lets you set the method, headers and body, such as httpie.io/app, or requests.post in Python.

fail_if: Says the URL is wrong
Says Groq is down

pairs.question: Before submitting any workflow, Aarav's UI sends GET /aarav/diagnoses and gets 200 OK with []. His teammate says "the API works but diagnosis is broken". What actually happened?

key_points.text: 200 means the request was understood and fine, not that you got what you wanted.
The list is empty because nothing has been created yet. Read only fetches what already exists.
Aarav needs to Create first (POST), which should return 201 Created.

fail_if: Says the server or the diagnosis logic is broken

pairs.question: Your Groq-backed app worked all morning. At 11:00 every request gets 429 with retry-after: 20. Nothing in your code changed. What happened, and is retrying immediately in a loop a good fix?

key_points.text: Too many requests: the account's rate limit is used up. The limit belongs to the account, not the key.
Wait the retry-after seconds. Retrying immediately just produces more 429s.
If the key is shared or leaked, everyone holding it draws from the same limit.

fail_if: Blames Groq's server or treats it as a 5xx

pairs.question: Your backend calls Groq, and the user sees 500 Internal Server Error from your backend. A teammate starts rewriting the JSON body the frontend sends. Why might that be the wrong place to look, and where do you look first?

key_points.text: A first digit of 5 means a server failed. A bad body would usually come back as 400.
This 500 comes from your own backend, so check its logs and code first: for example a missing GROQ_API_KEY environment variable, or an error from Groq that the backend doesn't handle.
A 4xx is the code that points at what was sent.

fail_if: Insists the frontend body is the cause

pairs.question: Aarav's key worked yesterday. Today, after he pasted it in a Discord help post, every request gets 401. He keeps resending the same request. What happened, and what should he do, in order?

key_points.text: The key leaked and was revoked (or must be). A bearer key works for anyone who copies it.
Revoke it, create a new one, then update every place it's used. Anything still sending the old key gets 401, which shows what was missed.
Deleting the post comes last, not first. Once a key has been seen, assume it was copied.

fail_if: The only fix is deleting the post
He keeps using the same key

pairs.question: You copy Groq's quickstart exactly and get: "Error 404. The model llama-3.3-70b-versatile does not exist or you do not have access to it." Your teammate says Groq's API is down today. What is the code telling you, what is the message telling you, and what do you change?

key_points.text: A 4xx means the mistake is in your request, not Groq's servers. If Groq were down you would expect a 5xx.
The message says what was not found: the model. The code says whose fault it is; the message says what.
Change the model name to one that exists, such as openai/gpt-oss-120b.

fail_if: Agrees Groq is down
Says the URL or endpoint is wrong

pairs.concept: Prompt plus input forms the package
pairs.question: The content sent to the model is: "Here is the workflow of an analyst working at an IT company in India. Diagnose and generate a plan to automate this work, or a part of the work." followed by Aarav's pasted workflow. Which part do you own, which part changes every request, and when plans come back bad, which part do you work on?

key_points.text: The instruction is yours and stays the same. The workflow is the user's and changes every time.
Both travel together in one content field as the package.
When outputs are bad you improve the instruction (the prompt), judged against the golden pair. It is the valuable part, refined by talking to real users.

fail_if: Says to change the user's workflow text to get better plans

pairs.question: Aarav's Diagnosis Service gave the same diagnosis twice for the same workflow. The model on Groq gave two different plans for the same request. Which one is deterministic, and how does that change the way you test each one?

key_points.text: The service is deterministic: same input, same output, every time. The model is probabilistic.
The deterministic part can be checked by rule, comparing exact output. The model's output can't be matched word for word, so it is checked with a written verifier against the golden pair.

fail_if: Says the model is deterministic
Says you test both by exact match

pairs.source: Lecture 4 notes, step 7; Lecture 5 notes, section 02

pairs.question: Your app uses the Groq SDK, and nowhere in your code do you see a URL or the word POST. One morning every call fails because the model you use was retired. Your teammate pastes the error into ChatGPT again and again. How does knowing what the SDK hides help you fix it faster?

key_points.text: The SDK wraps the address, action, key and package. Hidden machinery does not disappear.
Knowing that, you read the status code and message (404, model not found) and change the model name, instead of guessing.
Each round of pasting errors without understanding adds debt, until the AI can no longer fix what you can't explain.

fail_if: Says to switch to another SDK as the fix

pairs.source: Lecture 5 notes, section 12; Lecture 6 notes, section 02

pairs.question: You were asked to fill in one line, the process, in a working Gradio template. You paste the task into an AI. The code it returns runs, but it renamed your functions, swapped the interface and added ten parameters nobody asked for. Why is that a red flag, even though it works?

key_points.text: Extra, unrequested structure is the fingerprint of pasting the task into an AI without understanding it.
You can't verify code you don't understand, and every unrequested change is something else that can break.
Ask first: what is the smallest change that makes this work?

fail_if: Says it is fine because it runs

pairs.question: Without writing code, describe what your requests.post call to Groq must contain: what goes in the URL, the headers and the JSON body, and which part of the reply you show Aarav.

key_points.text: URL: the full endpoint, https://api.groq.com/openai/v1/chat/completions, sent with POST.
Headers: Authorization: Bearer with the key read from the environment.
Body: JSON with the model (openai/gpt-oss-120b) and messages, where the content is your prompt plus Aarav's workflow.
From the JSON reply, extract the message content and show only that.

recitation_flags: send a request to the API
fail_if: Puts the key in the body or the URL
Uses GET

pairs.question: To make it work quickly, you write the key directly in diagnose.py and push the repo to public GitHub for review. What happens next, and how should the code get the key instead?

key_points.text: Anyone who reads the repo now has the key and can use it as you, so it must be revoked and replaced.
The code should read it from an environment variable, such as os.environ["GROQ_API_KEY"], set outside the code (export in the terminal, a .env file that is never committed, or the host's settings).
Commit a .env.example with the variable names but no values, so others know what to set.

fail_if: Says making the repo private later is enough
Commits the .env file

pairs.source: Lecture 4 Keys guide; Lecture 5 notes, section 13; Lecture 8 notes, section 10

pairs.question: Your mentor asks you to switch Aarav's app from Groq to OpenAI for a day. You call the API with raw requests.post, not an SDK. What do you change, and what stays exactly the same?

key_points.text: Change the address (OpenAI's endpoint), the key (an OpenAI key in its own environment variable) and the model name.
The shape stays the same: POST, an Authorization header, a JSON body with the model and messages. No new package to install.

fail_if: Says the whole integration must be rewritten

pairs.question: diagnose(workflow) works when you run it in your terminal. Now Gradio, running on Aarav's laptop, needs to call it. What do you add, and what are the action, address and package of your new API?

key_points.text: Put the function behind a route with FastAPI: a decorator that names the action and address, such as @app.post("/api/diagnose").
Package: {"workflow": "..."} in, {"plan": "..."} out. The Groq key stays on the server and never goes to Gradio.
Deploy it so it has a URL other machines can reach.

fail_if: Gives Gradio the Groq key

pairs.question: Your /api/diagnose route promises: send a workflow, get a plan. Someone sends {"text": "..."} instead, and someone else sends an image. What happens without Pydantic, and what happens with a WorkflowIn model that says workflow must be text?

key_points.text: Without it, your code receives something it doesn't expect and throws, so the caller gets a 500 and you get a crash.
With it, the request is rejected at the door with an error that names the rule broken, before your function runs.
Policy versus enforcement: the route states the rule, Pydantic is the traffic police that enforces it.

fail_if: Says FastAPI accepts it and the model handles it

pairs.question: After vercel --prod, you POST to https://myapp.vercel.app and get 404. You fix that and get 500, and the Logs tab shows the Groq call failing. A friend suggests pasting the key into the code to make it go away. What is each code telling you, and what is the right fix?

key_points.text: 404: the deploy URL alone is not the route. Add /api/diagnose.
500: the right address, but the server failed, because the key isn't on that machine. Add GROQ_API_KEY in Vercel's environment variables with the exact name, then redeploy.
Hardcoding the key would undo the whole point: it would be in the repo for anyone to read.

fail_if: Agrees to hardcode the key

pairs.question: Your API works perfectly on your laptop, so you send Aarav http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/diagnose. He says it doesn't open. Why, and what does going to production actually change in your code?

key_points.text: 127.0.0.1 means "this machine". On Aarav's laptop it points at his own machine, where your server isn't running.
Production needs a deployed link. The code stays the same; only the address changes, from the local URL to the vercel.app one.

fail_if: Says his firewall or browser is the problem

pairs.question: Why not just run your API on your own laptop and leave it on? Suppose your link gets shared in a 2,000-person cohort channel.

key_points.text: Shut the laptop and the app is gone. One machine's memory and bandwidth can't serve thousands of users, so it falls over.
Running your own server means you own its upkeep and every attack on an open port. Renting (Vercel) hands you a ready machine for what you use.
Renting abstracts where the machine is and how you control it. You still decide what it stores and how it serves the API.

fail_if: Says a laptop is fine for a public link

pairs.question: On Monday Aarav gets a plan. On Tuesday he types: "I implemented the plan, but hit a problem." The call returns 200 and the model replies, but it has no idea which plan he means. Why? Without using the word "database", what is the smallest fix?

key_points.text: Every request starts from nothing. The model and the API keep no memory between calls.
Keep a file such as memory.txt. After each reply, write who said what and when, then send it along with the prompt next time so the model reads yesterday first.

fail_if: Blames the 200 or the model being broken

pairs.question: The plans are small, so a teammate wants to store them in Aarav's browser storage and skip the server. Name two ways this goes wrong.

key_points.text: The user can wipe it, by clearing site data or switching device, and then the app forgets again.
Anyone with access to the browser can read it, so nothing private, and never a key, can live there.

fail_if: Says browser storage is fine for private data

pairs.question: Your code saves each plan with open("memory.txt", "w").write(line). After three requests the file holds only one line. What went wrong, and what are the steps in English?

key_points.text: "w" replaces the whole file each time, so each write erased the earlier lines.
Read what is already there first, add the new line with its timestamp, workflow and plan, then write it all back (or append).

fail_if: Says the file is being deleted by the server

pairs.question: memory.txt works fine when you test alone. At the hackathon, Jagan and Vineet submit at the same minute. One of their plans is missing from the file. What happened, and when does a file stop being enough?

key_points.text: A race condition: both read the file, both wrote it back, and the second write erased the first one's line.
A file is fine for one user, a few writes a day, or read-only data. Once several people write, use a database.

fail_if: Blames a network error

pairs.question: The curriculum site serves over 2,000 people from plain files with no database, and it never loses anything. Doesn't that prove memory.txt is fine for your hackathon app too?

key_points.text: No. The curriculum site is read-only: nobody writes, so nothing races and files scale fine.
Your app writes on every request from many users, and writing is the expensive, risky part.

fail_if: Agrees the file is fine for many writers

pairs.question: For Aarav's app, decide whether each is a thing (its own table) or a fact (a column): a conversation, "9:12 am", and the tone of a plan. When could tone stop being a fact?

key_points.text: A conversation is a thing: it can be created, read, updated and deleted on its own, and there can be many.
"9:12 am" is a fact. It only says when a message was sent, so it is a column on a message.
Tone is a fact on a plan today. It would become a thing if users could save and reuse named tones. What the product does with it decides.

fail_if: Makes "9:12 am" its own table

pairs.question: Conversations and messages need linking. A teammate adds a message_ids column on conversations. Why won't that work, and where does the link column go?

key_points.text: One conversation has many messages, but each message is in one conversation: one-to-many.
A cell holds one value, so the pointer goes on the many side: conversation_id on messages, holding the conversation's id.

fail_if: Keeps a list of ids in one cell

pairs.question: A workflow uses many tools, and Jira shows up in many workflows. You also want to store how often each workflow uses each tool. Where does "how often" live?

key_points.text: Both sides are many, so no single column can hold the link. It needs a third table, such as workflow_tools, with one row per pairing.
"How often" is a fact about the pairing, so it lives on the workflow_tools row.

fail_if: Puts how often on the tools table or the workflows table

pairs.question: You store each workflow's plan in a plan column on the workflows table. Aarav asks: "Show me every plan this workflow ever got, oldest first." What goes wrong, and how should it be stored?

key_points.text: Each new plan overwrites the cell, so only the latest survives.
History is a row, not a cell: each diagnosis gets its own row with workflow_id and created_at, so you can list them by workflow in time order.

fail_if: Suggests appending plans into the same cell

pairs.question: To link workflows to people, a teammate stores the user's name on each workflow. Two users named Mira sign up. What breaks, and what should the workflow hold instead?

key_points.text: Names repeat, so you can't tell whose workflow is whose.
Every row gets an id that never repeats (the primary key). The workflow holds user_id, pointing at that id.

fail_if: Suggests adding the surname or email as the link

pairs.source: Lecture 6 notes, section 10; Lecture 8 notes, section 04

pairs.question: Your Modelling Lab board has eight tables: users, conversations, messages, attachments, workflows, diagnoses, tools and workflow_tools. Your bet is that 6 of 10 early-career people map one repeated workflow and build an app. Which tables do you create first for the hackathon, and why not all eight?

key_points.text: Users, workflows and diagnoses: the least that tests the bet.
Store only what answers tomorrow's questions. Storing more costs money and risk, and the rest can wait until users need it.

fail_if: Creates all eight up front

pairs.source: Lecture 8 notes, section 04; Lecture 6 notes, section 08

pairs.question: Supabase gives you a publishable key and a secret key. To save time, a teammate puts the secret key in the Gradio frontend so it can write rows directly. What's the risk, and where does each key belong?

key_points.text: The secret key can read and write everything. In the frontend anyone can copy it and read or delete every user's data.
The secret key lives only on your server, in an environment variable. The publishable key is safe in a browser only once row level security is on.

fail_if: Says the publishable key is always safe in the browser

pairs.question: Mira signs up for Aarav's app. With the project URL and a key, select * from workflows returns Aarav's workflows too. What is missing, and what exactly does it check?

key_points.text: Row level security: a policy that limits each user to their own rows. Without one, anyone whose query gets through gets everything.
It checks that the logged-in user's id, auth.uid(), matches the row's owner column, such as user_id.
It needs login: each signed-up user gets a UID that the policy checks.

fail_if: Says filtering in the frontend is enough

pairs.question: You replace memory.txt with Supabase. Which parts of your code should change, which should not, and what are the address, action, key and package for saving a diagnosis?

key_points.text: Only the storage lines change, becoming an insert and a select. diagnose() and the FastAPI route stay the same, because storage is a separate module.
Address: <project-url>/rest/v1/diagnoses. Action: POST to create. Key: the secret key in the headers, from the server's environment. Package: the row as JSON, such as workflow_id and plan.

fail_if: Rewrites diagnose() or the route to use the database

pairs.question: Your app now has many users writing at once. Why move to Postgres rented from Supabase, rather than a smarter file or a Postgres server you run yourself?

key_points.text: A database is a file system with decades of fixes: safe concurrent writes, backups, and rolling back a bad write.
Your model of things, facts and links maps straight onto SQL tables, columns and foreign keys, which makes it easy to query.
With ten users, renting beats self-hosting: Supabase handles the upkeep and is free at that size.

fail_if: Says a file with locks is just as good for many writers
